title: Tokenized workload profiling for dynamic batcher heuristics
content:
Summary:

This note captures a focused experiment series where we profiled realistic tokenized workloads to evaluate a set of dynamic batcher heuristics that account for per-request token counts. The primary goal: reduce 95/99 latency for short/medium requests during mixed-token traffic while maintaining reasonable throughput and multi-tenant fairness.

Why this matters:
- Continuous batching assumes homogeneous per-request cost, but real traffic mixes short prompts (few tokens) and long generations (hundreds+ tokens).
- Traditional size/time batching penalizes short requests: they wait for batch fill and then suffer inflated tail latency when coalesced with long requests.
- We want heuristics that reason in token-cost space (virtual token budget, token-weighted timeouts) instead of purely request-count or wall-time windows.

Experiment setup:
- Cluster: 8x A100s (p4d-like); workloads replayed through the local replay harness (linked PR above).
- Baseline scheduler: hybrid-size-timeout (count-based coalesce with fixed 2ms min timeout, 12ms max timeout).
- New heuristics evaluated:
  1) Token-budget windowing (TBW): form batches until either request-count cap or aggregated virtual-token budget (e.g., 4096 tokens) is reached; per-request token estimate is from client metadata or first-chunk tokenizer pass.
  2) Token-weighted timeout (TWT): per-request timeout = base_timeout * sqrt(1 + token_count/64). That biases shorter requests to flush earlier.
  3) Urgency-credit demotion (UCD): tenants accumulate urgency credits; long-running tenants have demoted priority when they exceed a token-rate threshold.
  4) Emergency short-slotting (ESS): reserve a small number of slots (virtual slots) that flush immediately for requests < 64 tokens when occupancy > 70%.

Workloads:
- Synthetic mixed profile derived from production traces (anonymized):
  - 60% short requests (median 18 tokens, 99th 80 tokens), QPS contribution 55%
  - 30% medium (median 120 tokens, 99th 300 tokens)
  - 10% long (median 800 tokens, 99th ~1600 tokens)
- Multi-tenant sim: 12 tenants, heavy skew: top-2 tenants account for 45% of traffic.
- Stress variants: steady, burst (sustained 3x QPS for 40s), and microburst (10kreq/s spikes for 2s).

Metrics collected (per-experiment run):
- P50/P95/P99 latency, measured at request completion (generation end).
- First-byte latency (time to first token).
- GPU utilization and batch size distribution (mean, median, 90th).
- Tail fairness: delta in P95 between heavy and light tenants (per-tenant P95 difference).
- Throughput (tokens/s).
- Abort/shedding rate and queueing depth.

Key findings (summary numbers are medians across 5 runs):
- Baseline: P95_short=420ms, P99_short=860ms; P95_overall=660ms; mean batch size=14 reqs, mean token-batch=5200 tokens; GPU util=74%.

- TBW alone (budget=4096): P95_short=320ms (24% improvement), P99_short=710ms (17% improvement); P95_overall=610ms (7% improvement). Throughput tokens/s -2.5%. Observations: batch token count more consistent, fewer mixed short+long batches, but short-request starvation still visible when budget exhausted by long requests queued earlier.

- TWT alone: P95_short=295ms (30% improvement), P99_short=600ms (30% improvement), P95_overall=585ms. Mean batch size in reqs decreased to 11 (throughput -4%). TWT introduces variance in batch sizes and slightly lower GPU utilization (71%).

- TBW + TWT combined: P95_short=250ms (40% improvement vs baseline), P99_short=480ms (44% improvement), P95_overall=540ms. GPU util=70%, throughput tokens/s -5%. Best tail-latency tradeoff across short requests.

- TBW+TWT+ESS: P95_short=240ms, P99_short=460ms; marginal additional gains for short tail. CPU overhead for slot bookkeeping increased by ~0.7%. ESS prevented ~88% of short-request coalescence with long requests under high occupancy.

- UCD added: improved fairness metric (max tenant P95 delta reduced from 340ms to 170ms) but introduced a small penalty to top-tenant P95 (increase ~60ms). Net JVM/driver-side contention increased slightly under very heavy skew.

Tradeoffs observed:
- Throughput vs tail: token-aware heuristics consistently reduced short-request tail latency at the cost of a few percent throughput reduction (tokens/s). This is acceptable for API tiers that prioritize latency.
- Fairness: simply optimizing for short-request tails risks harming heavy tenants; UCD-style demotion is required to avoid headroom capture by long-generation tenants.
- Complexity and observability: token-budgeting needs reliable token estimates from clients or an efficient tokenizer pass. Inaccurate token estimates create mis-scheduling.

Microburst behavior:
- Baseline under microbursts: sharp P99 spikes (>1.6s), queue jitter amplified.
- TBW+TWT: microburst P99 reduced by ~35%; ESS prevented most short-request blowups. However, under extreme spikes the scheduler began shedding long requests once queue depth crossed emergency threshold. Shedding rate was 0.3% in our runs (acceptable).

Profiling notes (bottlenecks found):
- Scheduler path: per-request bookkeeping became CPU-bound when ESS slots were tracked with coarse locks. Switched to sharded atomics in the test harness for the final runs which reduced scheduler tail CPU by ~45%.
- Token estimation: naive client-side estimation for a small fraction of requests was off by >30% causing a handful of token-overfilled batches leading to kernel thrashing. Mitigation: validator stage in the coalescer that does a cheap tokenizer depth-1 pass for uncertain requests.
- Trace correlation: first-byte latency correlated strongly with whether a short request was coalesced with a long one (r=0.78).

Open hypotheses / follow-ups:
1) Adaptive budget sizing: allow TBW budget to auto-scale based on observed token-length distribution; run ablations to see if we can recover throughput without losing short-tail improvements.
2) Per-tenant token credits with soft decay: test if per-tenant tokens/sec windowing prevents long-tenant capture without harming overall utilization.
3) Hybrid early-flush predictor: ML model that predicts expected generation length after seeing the prompt and flushing probability; measure cost of false predictions.
4) Integrate TWT with rolling-percentile SLOs (not static base_timeout), so short-request timeouts shorten further when cluster is uncongested.

Action items / next steps:
- Add a light tokenizer pass in the coalescer for requests that lack client token estimates (FR: scheduler 0.2.1). Owner: Evan. Due: 2025-02-18.
- Implement sharded slot accounting for ESS in the production scheduler (PR prototype exists in GH link). Owner: Samir. Due: 2025-02-10.
- Run a 24h production canary of TBW+TWT+ESS on a small subset of dedicated capacity for latency-sensitive customers. Create canary runbook and rollback hooks. Owner: Maya. Due: 2025-02-28.
- Dashboarding: add token-batch histogram, per-tenant P95 delta, and ESS eviction counts. Owner: Observability team. Due: 2025-02-22.

Notes to reviewers:
- Numbers are from replayed, anonymized production traces; absolute numbers will vary in prod. Focus review on tradeoffs and the mitigation steps rather than raw percent changes.
- Concern: scheduler complexity increases operational surface; recommend keeping UCD off by default and pilot only for high-SLA tenants.

Appendix (short):
- Example TBW parameters tested: [2048, 4096, 8192] tokens. 4096 had best balance; 2048 improved short tail more but lowered throughput heavily for medium workloads.
- TWT parameters sweep: base_timeout in [1ms, 2ms, 4ms], sqrt scale factor tuned for lambda values [32, 64, 128].
- Microbenchmark: single-GPU isolated test shows token-based coalescing reduces variance in per-batch kernel execution time by ~22%.

End of note.

If you want I can extract a shorter executive summary or create the canary runbook skeleton as a follow-up doc.
